claim: Fahrenfort et al., 2025 shows the influence of non-perceptual criterion shifts on neural measures of consciousness.
source: In Fahrenfort et al., 2025 we show the influence of non-perceptual criterion shifts on neural measures of consciousness.
evidence: This is a self-referential claim about the content of the authors' own publication.

claim: It was already known that subjective measures are sensitive to criterion confounds.
source: We fully agree (and point out in our article) that it was already known that subjective measures are sensitive to criterion confounds, and we are happy to read that this is acknowledged by Sandberg and Overgaard in their comment (Sandberg and Overgaard, 2025).
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as established knowledge and cite Sandberg and Overgaard, 2025 as acknowledging this.

claim: Criterion effects reveal themselves as over- (or under-) estimations of both conscious and unconscious processing in tandem.
source: Several findings from our studies are novel, such as the fact that criterion effects reveal themselves as over- (or under-) estimations of both conscious and unconscious processing in tandem, and that this has tangible implications when analyzing real neural data.
evidence: The authors present this as a novel finding from their own studies.

claim: Criterion effects have tangible implications when analyzing real neural data.
source: Several findings from our studies are novel, such as the fact that criterion effects reveal themselves as over- (or under-) estimations of both conscious and unconscious processing in tandem, and that this has tangible implications when analyzing real neural data.
evidence: The authors present this as a novel finding from their own studies.

claim: The PAS category [0] refers to 'No experience. No impression of the stimulus is experienced. All answers are experienced as mere guessing.'
source: This statement is derived from the description of the PAS itself, stating that [0] refers to either: "No experience. No impression of the stimulus is experienced. All answers are experienced as mere guessing." (Overgaard et al., 2006)
evidence: This is directly cited from Overgaard et al., 2006 as the definition of the PAS category.

claim: The PAS category [0] refers to 'No experience'.
source: "No experience" (Sandberg et al., 2010)
evidence: This is directly cited from Sandberg et al., 2010 as the definition of the PAS category.

claim: The PAS category [0] refers to 'No experience: No subjective experience of the stimulus, not even the 'faintest sensation' that anything was presented at all. Not even a feeling that something might have been presented'.
source: "No experience: No subjective experience of the stimulus, not even the 'faintest sensation' that anything was presented at all. Not even a feeling that something might have been presented" (Overgaard and Sandberg, 2021)
evidence: This is directly cited from Overgaard and Sandberg, 2021 as the definition of the PAS category.

claim: The PAS category [0] is used in the literature to make claims about the existence of unconscious working memory and other claims regarding unconscious processing.
source: This indeed is how it is used in the literature, for example when making claims about the existence of unconscious working memory, and many other claims regarding unconscious processing (see references in our manuscript).
evidence: The authors reference their own manuscript for examples of this usage in the literature.

claim: 32 researchers advise against relying on subjective measures alone to establish evidence of unconscious processing.
source: They further underpin this by reference to the fact that 32 researchers advise against relying on subjective measures alone to establish evidence of unconscious processing (Stockart et al., 2024, p. 14).
evidence: This is cited from Stockart et al., 2024, p. 14.

claim: Most consciousness researchers believe that subjective measures - and the PAS specifically - are the best measures to check whether a stimulus is consciously perceived.
source: although we would like to note that a relatively recent survey has shown that most consciousness researchers believe that subjective measures - and the PAS specifically - are the best measures to check whether a stimulus is consciously perceived (Francken et al., 2022, Figure 4).
evidence: This is cited from Francken et al., 2022, Figure 4, which presents survey data.

claim: Sandberg et al., 2022 modeled behavioral data from subjective reports.
source: To support this idea, they reference a publication (Sandberg et al., 2022) in which they model behavioral data from subjective reports.
evidence: The authors describe the content of Sandberg et al., 2022.

claim: Sandberg et al., 2022 is not about neural measures of consciousness.
source: Their article is not about neural measures of consciousness, nor does it contain brain imaging data.
evidence: The authors describe what Sandberg et al., 2022 does not contain.

claim: Sandberg et al., 2022 does not contain brain imaging data.
source: Their article is not about neural measures of consciousness, nor does it contain brain imaging data.
evidence: The authors describe what Sandberg et al., 2022 does not contain.

claim: Fahrenfort et al.'s article uses empirical data from two EEG experiments.
source: Further, we use empirical data from two EEG experiments to support the claim that the effects that we model in a signal detection framework are not merely theoretical artifacts but can have real implications for claims regarding the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC).
evidence: The authors describe their own methodology.

claim: The effects modeled in a signal detection framework are not merely theoretical artifacts but can have real implications for claims regarding the neural correlates of consciousness.
source: Further, we use empirical data from two EEG experiments to support the claim that the effects that we model in a signal detection framework are not merely theoretical artifacts but can have real implications for claims regarding the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC).
evidence: The authors present this as a claim supported by their EEG data.

claim: The PAS is not exhaustive (i.e. it may or may not capture weak conscious experiences depending on the experimental context).
source: The only correspondence seems to be that we agree on the somewhat unreliable nature of the PAS response, when discussing the fact that the PAS is not exhaustive (i.e. it may or may not capture weak conscious experiences depending on the experimental context).
evidence: The authors state this as an agreed-upon fact about the PAS.

claim: Skewes et al., 2021 provided false performance feedback which also affected participants' accuracy.
source: However, that article is intrinsically very different from ours, because it provided false performance feedback, which also affected participants' accuracy.
evidence: The authors describe the methodology of Skewes et al., 2021.

claim: In Fahrenfort et al.'s experiments, only veridical feedback was provided.
source: In our experiments we only provided veridical feedback and specifically kept accuracy the same between conditions so that the effects are criterion specific and not related to general effects of sensitivity or other cognitive effects.
evidence: The authors describe their own experimental methodology.

claim: In Fahrenfort et al.'s experiments, accuracy was kept the same between conditions so that the effects are criterion specific and not related to general effects of sensitivity or other cognitive effects.
source: In our experiments we only provided veridical feedback and specifically kept accuracy the same between conditions so that the effects are criterion specific and not related to general effects of sensitivity or other cognitive effects.
evidence: The authors describe their own experimental design and its purpose.

claim: The experimental context determines whether the relative confounding effect of criterion placement is larger in neural measures of either conscious or unconscious processing.
source: Furthermore, we not only show that the experimental context influences report criteria, which should be well-known (although we contest that this is widely accepted given the lenient use of subjective measures in the literature), but we also show through simulation that the experimental context determines whether the relative confounding effect of criterion placement is larger in neural measures of either conscious or unconscious processing.
evidence: The authors present this as a finding from their simulations.

claim: The proper PAS labels were used throughout Fahrenfort et al.'s experiment and repeatedly shown to remind participants.
source: In our experiment, the proper PAS labels were used throughout the experiment and repeatedly shown to remind participants of what we specifically asked of them.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental procedure.

claim: Fahrenfort et al. only gave veridical feedback to experimentally create criterion shifts.
source: This might be true if we had provided participants with false feedback, which we did not. We only gave veridical feedback to experimentally create criterion shifts, the same shifts that Sandberg and Overgaard acknowledge also occur naturally in other contexts given their admission that the PAS is not an exhaustive measure.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methodology.

claim: Similar criterion shifts can be observed in experiments comparing experimental blocks with different base-rates of stimulus occurrence (e.g., more vs less targets) without punishment manipulations.
source: Indeed, one can observe similar criterion shifts in experiments comparing experimental blocks with different base-rates of stimulus occurrence (e.g., more vs less targets) without punishment manipulations (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2025; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2025 and Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023.

claim: Criterion shifts do not affect conscious experience.
source: These studies also reveal that such criterion shifts do not affect conscious experience.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from the cited studies (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2025; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023).

claim: Claims based on post-hoc sorting of subjective reports are not likely to agree across experimental contexts.
source: Claims based on post-hoc sorting of subjective reports are not likely to agree across experimental contexts, so that conclusions regarding the depth or extent of unconscious processing, or regarding the temporal or spatial profile of the NCC, vary considerably across the literature (Yaron et al., 2022).
evidence: This is presented as a claim supported by Yaron et al., 2022.

claim: Conclusions regarding the depth or extent of unconscious processing, or regarding the temporal or spatial profile of the NCC, vary considerably across the literature.
source: Claims based on post-hoc sorting of subjective reports are not likely to agree across experimental contexts, so that conclusions regarding the depth or extent of unconscious processing, or regarding the temporal or spatial profile of the NCC, vary considerably across the literature (Yaron et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from Yaron et al., 2022.

claim: There is a serious confound in neural activation patterns based on subjective measures.
source: With respect to subjective measures, this is not due to mere 'limitations', but due to a serious confound in neural activation patterns based on subjective measures, one that deserves considerable attention.
evidence: This is presented as a conclusion from the authors' work.

claim: The underlying assumption of the PAS is that selecting [0] will only occur if trials are 'truly' unseen.
source: In Fahrenfort et al., 2025 we state that the underlying assumption is that selecting [0] will only occur if trials are 'truly' unseen.
evidence: The authors state this as an assumption they identified in their work.

claim: The implication of accepting the validity of the PAS category [0] is that it measures what the label refers to, that the stimulus is 'truly' not experienced.
source: The implication of accepting the validity of this category is clearly that it measures what the label refers to, that the stimulus is 'truly' not experienced (although the exact phrasing of this category may vary slightly between studies).
evidence: This is presented as a logical inference from the definition of the PAS category.

claim: Sandberg and Overgaard claim that it is a niche position to suggest that 'awareness ratings should be treated as flawless insights into participants' experience'.
source: Sandberg and Overgaard now claim that it is a niche position to suggest that "awareness ratings should be treated as flawless insights into participants' experience", referring to their own care in highlighting that this implication is unwarranted (Sandberg and Overgaard, 2025).
evidence: This is cited from Sandberg and Overgaard, 2025.

claim: The current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice.
source: We made explicit that our criterion manipulation was strong ("As such, the current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice", page 13 top)
evidence: This is a self-referential quote from the authors' own manuscript.

claim: The PAS is a measurement instrument that refers to verbal labels of a scale.
source: The PAS refers to verbal labels of a scale, i.e. it is a measurement instrument.
evidence: This is presented as a definition or characterization of the PAS.

claim: Highlighting imperfections of subjective measures cannot serve as an argument in their defense.
source: We fail to see how highlighting imperfections of subjective measures can serve as an argument in their defense, or how these concerns disappear when acknowledging them.
evidence: This is a logical argument made by the authors about the implications of acknowledging limitations.

claim: Acknowledging imperfections of subjective measures does not make the concerns about them disappear.
source: We fail to see how highlighting imperfections of subjective measures can serve as an argument in their defense, or how these concerns disappear when acknowledging them.
evidence: This is a logical argument made by the authors.

claim: The continued use of subjective measures (with or without the acknowledgement of their imperfection) does not build support for their continued use.
source: Similarly, we fail to see how the continued use of subjective measures (with or without the acknowledgement of their imperfection) builds support for their continued use.
evidence: This is a logical argument made by the authors.

claim: Fahrenfort et al.'s article is specifically about the effect criterion shifts have on post-hoc sorted data to create neural conditions that are claimed to correspond to 'real' subjective states.
source: Our article is specifically about the effect criterion shifts have on post-hoc sorted data to create neural conditions that are claimed to correspond to 'real' subjective states (such as expressed in the labels of the PAS, or in a 'yes'/'no' response).
evidence: The authors describe the focus of their own article.

claim: The aim of Fahrenfort et al.'s paper was not to show that report criteria depend on experimental context.
source: More importantly, the aim of our paper was not to show that report criteria depend on experimental context.
evidence: The authors clarify what their paper's aim was not.

claim: Fahrenfort et al. took as a starting point that report criteria depend on experimental context to show the effect of this contextual change on neural correlates based on subjective measures and post-hoc sorting, including the PAS.
source: Rather, we took this as a starting point to show the effect of this contextual change on neural correlates based on subjective measures and post-hoc sorting, including the PAS.
evidence: The authors describe their methodological approach.

claim: A single sentence in the instructions ('Only press 0 if you are 100% convinced that no square appeared and only press 3 if you are 100% convinced that a square appeared.') might be misconstrued by participants as a general confidence rating.
source: Subsequently, after personal communication with them, we conceded that a particular sentence that Sandberg and Overgaard highlight and that occurred somewhere in the instructions ("Only press 0 if you are 100% convinced that no square appeared and only press 3 if you are 100% convinced that a square appeared.") might be misconstrued by participants as a general confidence rating.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as a potential issue raised by Sandberg and Overgaard.
